edges.effect_quant: The best overall reading is that more outdoor time clearly helps prevent myopia onset and may modestly slow refractive worsening at the population level, but the direct signal for already-myopic children is weaker. A 2017 meta-analysis found reduced myopic shift overall but no clean dose-response relationship for progression in existing myopes, while a 2024 Cochrane review of 10,733 children found small favorable changes in refractive error and axial length with school-based outdoor interventions but low-certainty evidence for progression suppression.
edges.population: children and adolescents exposed to higher outdoor time or school-based outdoor interventions
edges.mechanism: Outdoor light exposure may alter retinal dopamine signaling, reduce prolonged near-work intensity, and slow axial elongation pathways involved in myopic development. These mechanisms look stronger for delaying onset than for reversing established progression.
edges.summary: This edge should stay cautiously positive rather than overstated. Increasing outdoor time in children probably helps with the broader myopia trajectory and may modestly slow progression, but the evidence for already-myopic children is less decisive than the evidence for prevention of onset.
edges.caveats: Much of the literature mixes onset prevention with progression outcomes, which can make the overall effect look stronger than it is for established myopes alone. School-based interventions are also behavior packages, so the precise dose of outdoor exposure is hard to isolate.
